# Names and aliases: research brief

You are filling in the name and aliases of people in a Marvel watch-tracker app's character indexes (the Raft for villains, the Compound
for heroes). Accuracy is the whole job: every claim must hold up against what is actually said on screen.

## Your input

`chunkNN.json` (the number is in your task): a list of people. Each person has `universe` (which universe tab they're on) and `files`: one
file, or two when the same person has a hero file (`tag` "A") and a villain file (`tag` "T"). Each file has:
- `id`
- `n`: the current file title. Either a string, or a staged list `[[value, title], ...]`: the app shows the last value whose title the
  viewer has watched.
- `k`: a short description (same staging).
- `steps`: `[sentence, title]` pairs, in story order: every title this person is on screen in.

`alltitles.json` is the list of every title the app knows. Any title you output must match an entry there EXACTLY (seasons are separate
titles, e.g. "Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D. S3", "Loki S1", "What If...? S2").

## The owner's rule (decided)

1. **A file is titled by the person's real name**, the same on their hero and villain file. Use the form the screen uses most:
   "Bucky Barnes", "Steve Rogers", "Sam Wilson", "Ava Starr", "Natasha Romanoff". If the current title is already the real name in a
   reasonable form, keep it exactly as it is (don't respell or lengthen it).
2. **If the real name is never said on screen** in any title the person appears in, keep the current title (usually the codename).
   "Said on screen" includes clearly shown on screen in writing (a file, a name tag) and a later title revealing it. It excludes comics,
   marketing, credits only, and wiki-only names.
3. **If the person is introduced under a codename and their real name is only said in a later title**, stage the name:
   `[[codename, first title], [real name, title where the real name is first said]]`. The current title may already be staged like this
   (e.g. Sharon Carter: Agent 13, then Sharon Carter); keep correct stagings.
4. **Aliases**: every codename, hero or villain name, or cover identity said on screen for this person: "Ghost", "The Winter Soldier",
   "White Wolf", "Falcon", "Captain America", "Spider-Man", "Natalie Rushman" (Natasha's cover in Iron Man 2), "Yellowjacket", "Mysterio".
   - NOT aliases: nicknames and short forms ("Cap", "Nat", "Bucky" for James), ranks and titles ("Director", "King", "Sorcerer Supreme",
     "Agent"), descriptions ("the Avenger"), names from comics or marketing never said on screen ("Nomad" for Steve is never said:
     exclude it).
   - Each alias carries the title where it is first said on screen **for this person** (among the titles they appear in, or a title that
     names them on screen). That title reveals it, so it must not be earlier than the first time it's said: a too-early title spoils.
   - If the real name is the title, the codename goes in aliases. If the codename stays the title (real name never said), list only
     OTHER aliases (not the title itself).
   - Order aliases by the order they are revealed.
5. Different universes are different people: a 1994 cartoon's Captain America is Steve Rogers only if that show says so.
6. No em dashes anywhere in what you write.

## Sources

Verify each claim yourself; don't guess from memory. Use:
- Wikipedia raw pages: `curl -s "https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=<Page>&action=raw"`
- Fan wikis, only through their API (their /wiki/ pages return 403):
  `curl -s "https://<wiki>.fandom.com/api.php?action=parse&page=<Page>&prop=wikitext&format=json"` with wiki one of
  marvelcinematicuniverse, marvel, spiderman, xmenmovies, marvelanimated, sonys-spider-man-universe. The MCU wiki's character pages have
  an "Aliases" field and often quotes; check the alias is really said on screen and in which title (episode transcripts and quotes help).
- Space requests a second or two apart (Wikipedia answers 429 when rushed). Never put personal information in a request.
- Fan wiki alias lists include comics and tie-in names: check each one is actually said in a film or episode.

Most people in a chunk will have no aliases and a title that is already their name: that's expected. Spend your effort on the ones that
have codenames.

## Output

Write `outNN.json` (same number) in the same folder: a JSON list with **one entry per person in the chunk, in the same order**:

```json
{"ids": ["bucky-barnes", "winter-soldier"],
 "name": "Bucky Barnes",
 "aliases": [["The Winter Soldier", "Captain America: The Winter Soldier", "<source url>"], ["White Wolf", "Black Panther", "<source url>"]],
 "changed": true,
 "note": "Raft file was titled The Winter Soldier; real name said in The Winter Soldier itself."}
```

- `name`: a string, or a staged list `[[value, title], ...]`.
- `aliases`: `[]` when none.
- `changed`: true if `name` differs from any of the person's current file titles (`n`), or aliases is non-empty.
- `note`: a few words, only when something changed or you were unsure. Put open doubts here starting with "UNSURE:".
- Every title must be in alltitles.json exactly.

When done, reply with just: how many people, how many changed, and the UNSURE ones (ids and why).

# Names and aliases: independent re-check

Another researcher proposed names and aliases for people in a Marvel watch-tracker app's character indexes. Your job is to try to
**disprove** each claim. Assume nothing in the proposal is right until you have checked it against sources. You have the claims and the
files, not the researcher's reasoning.

## Input (in this folder)

- `chunkNN.json`: the people (each with `files`: `id`, current title `n`, description `k`, `steps` = `[sentence, title]` for every title
  the person is on screen in).
- `outNN.json`: the proposal, one entry per person, same order: `ids`, `name` (string, or staged `[[value, title], ...]`), `aliases`
  (`[[alias, title, source], ...]`), `changed`, `note`.
- `alltitles.json`: every title the app knows.

## The rule the proposal must follow

1. A file is titled by the person's real name (the form the screen uses most), the same on hero and villain files. If the current title is
   already the real name in a reasonable form, it stays exactly as it is.
2. A real name never said on screen (comics, marketing, credits-only or wiki-only) doesn't count: the current title stays.
3. A real name first said in a later title is staged: `[[codename, first title], [real name, title where it's first said]]`.
4. Aliases: codenames, hero or villain names, and cover identities said on screen for this person. Not nicknames or short forms ("Cap",
   "Nat"), ranks or titles ("Director", "King", "Sorcerer Supreme"), descriptions, or names never said on screen. Each alias's title is the
   first title where it is said on screen for this person; it must not be earlier (that would spoil it). If the codename stays the title, it
   is not repeated in aliases.
5. Different universes are different people.
6. Every title must match alltitles.json exactly; no em dashes.

## What to check, for EVERY entry

- Changed or aliased entries: is the real name really said on screen? In that form? Is each alias really said on screen for THIS person
  (not a different character, not a comic name)? Is the alias's title the first title it's said in, and not earlier? Is a staging title
  right?
- Unchanged entries: skim for misses: a person whose title is a codename although their real name is said on screen, or an obvious alias
  that was left out (e.g. a hero name).
- Format: titles in alltitles.json, aliases not duplicating the title, no nicknames or ranks.

Sources: Wikipedia raw pages (`curl -s "https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=<Page>&action=raw"`) and fan wikis only through their API
(`curl -s "https://<wiki>.fandom.com/api.php?action=parse&page=<Page>&prop=wikitext&format=json"`, wiki one of marvelcinematicuniverse,
marvel, spiderman, xmenmovies, marvelanimated, sonys-spider-man-universe). Space requests a second or two apart. Fan wiki alias lists mix in
comics: check the screen.

## Output

Write `checkNN.json` (same number) in this folder: a JSON list of verdicts for entries you dispute or correct ONLY (agreeing entries are
left out):

```json
{"ids": ["..."], "verdict": "wrong" | "fix" | "missing" | "unsure",
 "what": "name" | "alias" | "title",
 "claim": "the claim you dispute (copy it)",
 "correct": "what it should be, in the output format (a name, or an alias as [alias, title]); null to drop it",
 "why": "one or two sentences, with the source url"}
```

Then reply with just: entries checked, how many disputed, and the three most serious.

# Names and aliases: the revision (the owner's corrected rule)

A first pass gave every person in a Marvel watch-tracker's character indexes (the Raft for villains, the Compound for heroes) a title and
a list of aliases. It applied the rule far too strictly: it only counted names *spoken aloud on screen*, and so left out things every
viewer knows. The owner's words: "It does not have to only be explicitly said on screen to count. Captain Marvel is the name of the movie.
She was literally a captain in the movie. Its everywhere. Mole Man's name is only ever Harvey Elder. Laura IS X-23. Victor von Doom is
ALWAYS Doctor Doom. By applying rules after rules with no leniency you make things worse by not capturing the full context."

Your job: produce the corrected result for your chunks, using judgment and the full context.

## The rule now

1. **A file is titled by the person's real name**, the same on their hero and villain file. Use the form people know ("Bucky Barnes",
   "Steve Rogers", "Ava Starr", "Harvey Elder"). Keep the current title's form when it's already the real name. If a version's real name is
   truly unknown for that version (nobody, not the title, credits or marketing, ties a real name to it), the codename stays the title.
2. **A name or alias counts when the title establishes it for this version of the character in any clear way**: said or shown on screen,
   the title's own name (Captain Marvel in "Captain Marvel", Ironheart in "Ironheart", Doctor Strange in "Doctor Strange"), its credits, its
   official marketing, or simply because it's the famous identity this version clearly is (Victor von Doom is Doctor Doom; Laura is X-23;
   Carol Danvers is Captain Marvel from her own film; Riri Williams is Ironheart; Reed Richards is Mister Fantastic; Bruce Banner is the
   Hulk; Obadiah Stane's suit is the Iron Monger; Thaddeus Ross becomes the Red Hulk; Samuel Sterns is the Leader; Brock Rumlow is
   Crossbones).
3. **What still doesn't count**:
   - fan-made names, and names from a different version that this version never becomes (a comics codename the film's character never
     takes up);
   - casual nicknames and short forms ("Cap", "Nat", "Tony" for Anthony): an established moniker is fine ("Doc Ock", "Black Mariah");
   - ranks and titles in the alias list ("Director", "King", "Sorcerer Supreme"): don't add them as aliases;
   - posing as another real, specific person (Zemo as Dr. Broussard, Talos as Fury): not an alias; a made-up cover identity kept up for a
     while (Natalie Rushman) is; a one-off fake name in a single scene isn't;
   - anything false for this version: **a separate being keeps its own file and its own name** (the Sony Venom symbiote is "Venom", not
     Eddie Brock, and Eddie doesn't get "Venom" as an alias; Mayhem is Brigid's split-off double; judge others like the Phoenix Force or
     White Vision the same way: one body and mind is one person, a separate being is not).
4. **When an alias is revealed**: the first title in this person's file where the identity is theirs (Carol: Captain Marvel at "Captain
   Marvel"; Sam: Captain America at "The Falcon and the Winter Soldier", not before he takes the shield). Never earlier than the title where
   they actually take it on: that would spoil it. A staged real name works the same way:
   `[[codename, first title], [real name, title where the real name becomes known]]`, only when the real name truly comes out later.
5. **Group files keep their own titles.** If a group file (e.g. "pr-st-pride", PRIDE) was attached to a person's entry, leave it out of
   the person's `ids` and don't rename it.
6. Different universes are different people. Every title must match alltitles.json exactly (seasons are separate titles). No em dashes.
7. **Open owner calls, leave as the first pass has them** (I'll settle them with the owner): Killmonger's name (N'Jadaka or Erik Stevens),
   and ranks inside titles ("Father Delgado", "Colonel Chester Phillips", "Sir Nicholas Fury").

## Input (in this folder)

For each of your chunk numbers NN:
- `chunkNN.json`: the people and their files (`id`, `tag` "A" hero / "T" villain, title `n`, description `k`, `steps` = every title they're
  on screen in).
- `outNN.json`: the first pass (one entry per person, same order: `ids`, `name`, `aliases` `[[alias, title, source]]`, `changed`, `note`).
- `checkNN.json` if it exists: an independent re-check's disputes of the first pass. It used the same over-strict rule, so take its factual
  corrections (a wrong person, a wrong title, a separate being merged) and ignore its "not said aloud, drop it" verdicts where the rule
  above says the name counts.

Sources when you need them: Wikipedia raw (`curl -s "https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=<Page>&action=raw"`), fan wikis through
their API (`curl -s "https://<wiki>.fandom.com/api.php?action=parse&page=<Page>&prop=wikitext&format=json"`; marvelcinematicuniverse,
marvel, spiderman, xmenmovies, marvelanimated, sonys-spider-man-universe). Space requests a second or two apart. But most of this is
judgment about what the title plainly establishes: you won't need a source for "Laura is X-23".

## What to look at

Go through EVERY person, not only the first pass's changes:
- every title that's a codename while the real name is known for this version (from the screen, credits or marketing);
- every famous identity left out or dropped because it wasn't "said aloud";
- every alias revealed too late because of the strict rule (Captain Marvel at Far From Home is wrong: it's "Captain Marvel");
- every first-pass alias that is actually wrong for this version (separate beings, impersonations, nicknames).

## Output

Write `finalNN.json` for each of your chunks: same format as `outNN.json`, one entry per person in chunk order (drop group files from
`ids`), aliases as `[alias, title]` (no source needed), plus a `rev` field only where you changed the first pass: a few words saying what and
why. When done, reply with: per chunk, how many entries you revised, and anything you think the owner should decide.
